catalog_quote: It seems that Bora does not have a stress system aside from the system of tone. We do not discount the possibility that Bora’s tone system is a stress system implemented on tone. See note 8, page 98 for further discussion. ... Bora—it seems—has no stress system aside from the system of tone: there do not seem to be stressed versus unstressed syllables, only high tone versus low tone syllables. In basic design, the Bora tone system is not unlike the accentual system of Lithuanian described by Kenstowicz (1994:584ff.). We do not discount the possibility that Bora’s tone system is a stress system implemented on tone. ... 1. There are two tones, high (H) and low (L). The marked tone is low. The general default tone is high (although the default for final syllables is low). 2. A sequence of two low tones is disallowed except at the end of a word or tonal phrase. sweep_summary: Bora (bora1263) is in the catalog as 'tonal' on Thiesen & Weber 2012 (no stress system apart from tone; possibly stress implemented on tone). All three title-keyword items are the Seifart/Meyer drummed-speech (manguaré) studies: Meyer, Dentel & Seifart 2012 Interspeech (fetched sources open from ISCA, read: inter-beat durations track vowel-to-vowel intervals; Bora presupposed two-tone; no word on stress) and Seifart et al. 2018 R. Soc. Open Sci. (fetched sources open via Europe PMC full-text XML, read: 'Bora is a two-tone language, i.e. every syllable is associated with either high or low tone', light/heavy mora distinction; 'stress' appears only in the general literature review) are prosody-but-not-word-stress; the 2018 paper confirms the two-tone basis of the coding, the 2012 paper is silent. Seifart & Meyer 2010 is an unpublished DGfS talk with no locatable text (Glottolog record saved; The only first-hand word-stress statement read is Roe 2014 (already on file from the 9/16 audit), pp. 79 and 100: 'mixed tone/stress system', penultimate stress in 2-3-syllable words, antepenultimate in longer words, 'Tone is the only indicator of stress in Bora' — a reanalysis that refines, not supersedes, the deciding source. No recode indicated.

new_statements.quote: As mentioned in Chapter 1, Bora has a mixed tone/stress system. In addition to the underlying tone pattern of the noun root, Bora assigns low tones to stressed syllables. (Tone is the only indicator of stress in Bora.) ... Two and three syllable nouns have low tone on the penultimate syllable, which I analyze as a stress marker. [p. 79] ... In Bora, low tones associate to stressed syllables. Two and three syllable words have penultimate stress, while words longer than three syllables have antepenultimate stress. OCP conflicts occur when stressed syllables are adjacent to low-toned syllables. Word-medially, Bora resolves these conflicts by deleting the low stress marker. [p. 100]

new_statements.reading: Roe reanalyses the positional low tones of Bora as a stress marker: penultimate 'stress' in 2-3-syllable words, antepenultimate in longer words, weight-blind, exponent = L tone only, deleted under OCP clash with lexical L. Her acoustic chapter measures correlates of H vs L tone, not of stressed vs unstressed syllables, so this is an analytic reinterpretation of the same facts Thiesen & Weber describe, i.e. exactly the 'stress system implemented on tone' possibility their deciding quote leaves open. It refines rather than overturns the catalog's 'tonal' coding; the three sweep items add nothing on word stress (two are silent or confirm two-tone, one is an unlocatable talk).

audit.recode_to: No recode of 'kind' recommended. Add Roe 2014 to the record's contra/caution: 'Roe (2014: xiv, 79, 100) reanalyses the positional low tones as stress: penultimate in 2-3-syllable words, antepenultimate in longer words, tone being the only exponent of stress.' If the catalog's convention codes tonally-realised predictable prominence as stress, the alternative coding would be a right-edge window (penult <=3 syll / antepenult otherwise, weight-insensitive, L-tone exponent) flagged as analysis-dependent.

sources.quote: Importantly for the study of manguaré, Bora is a two-tone language, i.e. every syllable is associated with either high (H, e.g. bá) or low (L, e.g. bà) tone [12], which are expressed by fundamental frequency pitch contours (figure 3a). ... Bora phonology distinguishes light, i.e. mono-moraic (C)V syllables from heavy, i.e. bi-moraic (C)VC and (C)VV syllables for various phonotactic and morphophonological purposes [12].
sources.locator: sec. 1.5 'Bora phonology'; sec. 4 Discussion ('we found four distinct rhythmic units... V < VC < VVC < VCC')
sources.note: No statement on Bora word stress. The paper (Seifart is a first-hand Bora/Miraña fieldworker) describes Bora as a two-tone language, every syllable H or L, citing Thiesen & Weber 2012 [12], with a light/heavy (mora) syllable distinction; the drummed form encodes the two tones plus vowel-to-vowel interval duration (V < VC < VVC < VCC). Every occurrence of 'stress' is in the general literature review (isochrony, stress placement and syllable weight in other languages), never a claim about Bora stress. Confirms the two-tone analysis the catalog's coding rests on; silent on whether a stress syste…

sources.citation: Meyer, Julien, Laure Dentel & Frank Seifart. 2012. A methodology for the study of rhythm in drummed forms of languages: application to Bora Manguaré of Amazon. Proc. Interspeech 2012, 687–690. doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2012-210
sources.quote: According to previous publications, Manguaré drums emulate formulaic sentences and each beat represents the tones of a syllable (Bora having two contrastive tones (H and L)) [10]. ... Bora language has six phonemic vowels positions in addition to a phonemic distinction of vowel length ... The syllable structure of Bora is (C)V(C) ... The four main syllable types are thus (C)V, (C)Vː, (C)Vh, and (C)Vʔ [11]. ... we showed that the inter-beat durations played by the Bora drummers corresponded to V-to-V intervals rather than to syllables of the associated spoken utterances.
sources.locator: sec. 1.2 'The Manguaré drummed form and the Bora language', p. 687–688; sec. 3.2 and Conclusion, p. 689–690
sources.note: Nothing on word stress or accent placement. The paper is a durational (inter-beat interval) study of the manguaré drummed form of Bora; it presupposes Bora as a two-tone (H/L) language, measures vowel-to-vowel interval durations (V < VC < VV/CCV) and an effect of the tonal duplet (LH shortest, LL/HL longest) on inter-beat duration. 'Rhythm' in the title means segmental timing, not metrical stress. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the paper.
